column2: Then Death spoke again to the blessed Grandfather: "God, I would not take the subjects; again I appease you."
To her, afraid of adharma and asking again, the god of gods then, restraining that word, said:

There is no adharma for you, Death; restrain the subjects, auspicious one; what I have said, good one, will not be false; nothing will come of it here.

Thus addressed, great king, she said again with folded hands to the great-souled imperishable lord of gods, "No."
The god then said to her, "Death, destroy mankind; there will be no adharma for you, and I shall support you, auspicious one.
The drops of tears that I saw fall, those held in the hands before, will be diseases of dreadful form for men and, when the time comes, will afflict them, Death.
At the end of life of all creatures you shall join desire and anger together; thus immeasurable dharma will come to you, and you will not gain adharma, being of equal conduct.
Thus you will guard dharma as told, and not sink yourself in adharma; therefore take as your wish what has come, and, joining them, destroy creatures here."
She then, afraid of the curse, from the name "Death," said to him, "So be it." Then at the end of life, at the end of creatures' breaths, reaching desire and anger, she bewilders and kills.
Death, those diseases, those falls of tears, by which men's bodies are pained, belong to all creatures at the end of breath; therefore do not grieve; understand by intellect.
All the gods, going at the end of breath of creatures, return and come back likewise; so all men, at the end of breath, having gone, return like gods, lion among kings.

The wind, terrible, of terrible sound, of great power, is the breath of all creatures; his livelihood is varied at the breaking of the bodies of the embodied; therefore the wind is the god of gods, excellent.
All the gods are excellent by the name of mortals; all mortals are excellent by the name of gods; therefore do not grieve for your son, lion among kings; your son, having reached heaven, rejoices.
Thus Death was made by the god for the subjects, gathering them rightly when the time comes; and her diseases, the falls of tears, gather creatures here when the time comes."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Is this dharma for aims here or for aims hereafter, or is dharma for both? Tell me, grandsire."
[Bhishma said:] "Good conduct, tradition and the Vedas are the threefold mark of dharma; the wise call wealth the fourth mark of dharma.
Even the actions spoken of are decided in the later and the earlier; the rule of dharma was made here for the course of the world; it brings happiness as its result both here and hereafter.
Not gaining skill in dharma, the sinful cling to sin, and some sinners are not freed from sin in calamity.
When one becomes a knower of dharma he becomes blameless; the end of dharma is one's own conduct; relying on that alone you will know.
When a thief, possessed by adharma, takes wealth, he delights in carrying off another's goods where there is no king.
When others carry off his, then he wants a king; then he envies those who are content with their own wealth.
The fearless, pure man goes to the king's door unsuspecting; for he sees no bad conduct at all within himself.
No one is utterly mighty or happy; therefore your mind should never be set on crookedness.
He has no fear of the wicked, nor of thieves, nor of the king; doing nothing to anyone, he may dwell fearless and pure.
The thief suspects everywhere, like a deer come to a village; sin done in many ways he sees elsewhere.
The glad and pure go everywhere ever fearless, for they see no bad conduct of their own in others.
It must be given: this dharma is spoken by those devoted to the good of beings; the wealthy think it started by the wretched.
When wretchedness is restrained, then it pleases them; no one is utterly wealthy or happy.
What a man does not wish others to do to himself, he should not do to others, knowing what is unpleasant to himself.
One who is the paramour of another's wife, what can he say to anyone? My view is that he would not endure it if another did that to him.
He who himself wishes to live, how can he have another killed? Whatever one wishes for oneself, he should consider for others too.
He should share surplus enjoyments with others who have nothing; for this reason the Creator started usury.
It should be so that the gods keep to the agreement; and if there is steadiness in dharma at the time of gain, that is also fair.
The wise say dharma is all that is accepted as dear; see this mark in dharma and adharma, Yudhishthira.
Ordained by the Creator long ago, joined with the support of the world, fixed in subtle dharma and wealth, is the highest conduct of the good.
This mark of dharma has been told to you, best of the Kurus; therefore your mind should never be set on crookedness."
[Yudhishthira said:] "The many questions in my heart you have answered; I shall ask you another, king, not as in a quarrel.
These bring one to, create and carry across; dharma cannot be known, Bharata, by rote.
One dharma is for one in a level state, another for one in an uneven; how can calamities be known by reading?

Someone is seen to practise adharma in the form of dharma, a common man, and someone not common practising dharma in the form of adharma.

The dharmas of the Krita are one, of the Treta another, of the Dvapara another, and in the Kali as if done as far as possible.
The word of tradition is true: this is the gathering of the world; beyond the traditions the Vedas spread facing every way.
Some from desire, some from decay, some for other reasons; many of the bad follow vain conduct.
Dharma is soon dissolved among the good; others call them mad and even laugh at them.
Great men have returned, resorting to the dharma of kings; for no conduct is seen that is for the good of all.
By that same one another prevails, and again oppresses another; and again he is seen of like form by chance.
By whatever one prevails over another, he oppresses others also; one should observe the lack of one-pointedness in all conduct.
Dharma long approached and cited by the wise: by that earlier conduct the order becomes eternal."
In the forest, a certain forest-dweller, a twice-born named Jajali, came to the seashore and performed great austerity.
Restrained, with restrained diet, wearing bark and deerskin and matted locks, bearing dirt and mud, the wise sage did so for many years.
Once, that sage of great splendour, living in water, roamed through the worlds with the speed of mind, seeing them.
Once, in the midst of the water, the sage thought, looking at the earth with its forests and groves up to the sea.
There is none like me here in the moving and unmoving world; who else could go with me through the water and the sky?
Seen by rakshasas in the midst of the water, he spoke so; and the pishachas said to him, "You ought not to speak so.
The merchant Tuladhara of Varanasi, of great fame, who follows a trader's dharma, does not deserve to speak as you do, best of the twice-born."
Thus addressed by the beings, the great ascetic Jajali replied, "I shall see that wise and famous Tuladhara."
[Yudhishthira said:] "What good deed did Jajali do before, by which he reached the highest success? You should tell us that."
[Bhishma said:] "He was joined with exceedingly fierce austerity, devoted to bathing in the river at dusk and dawn.
Tending the fires rightly, intent on study, knowing the rule of forest-dwelling, Jajali blazed with fortune.
Abiding in truth and austerity, he did not look to dharma; in the rains he slept under the open sky, in winter in water.
In summer he endured wind and heat, and did not find dharma; he slept on painful beds of many kinds and rolled on the ground.
Once, in the rains, the sage standing in the open took the water from the sky on his head again and again.
His locks became wet and matted, lord; from always going to the forest he was dirty, joined with dirt.
Once, fasting, living on wind, of great austerity, he stood like a log, untroubled, never moving.
As he stood like a post, motionless, Bharata, a pair of kulinga birds made a nest on his head, king.
The compassionate sage watched the pair making a nest there with straw and fibre in his locks.
When the great ascetic did not move at all, standing like a post, the two, trusting, lived there happily.
When the rains had passed and autumn arrived, the two flying creatures, bewildered by desire, by the Prajapatya rule of knowledge,
laid eggs on his head, king; the radiant brahmana of strict vows knew of the eggs.
Knowing, the great-splendoured Jajali did not move; his mind ever steady in dharma, he did not like adharma.
Day by day the two came to his head and, reassured, dwelt there, delighted then, lord.
From the nourished eggs the chicks were born and grew up there, and Jajali did not move.
Guarding the eggs of the kulingas, of controlled vow, the righteous-souled one stayed thus, motionless and collected.
Then in due time the birds came to be; and the sage knew the young birds had grown wings.
Then once, seeing those birds there, the one of controlled vows, best of the wise, became supremely pleased.
Likewise, seeing them grown, delighted, the two birds lived fearless there with their offspring.
He saw the winged ones fly off and come back each evening, and Jajali did not move.
Sometimes they came again and went again, abandoned by mother and father, and Jajali did not move.
Then, having gone to roam by day, the chicks returned in the evening to the same place for dwelling.
Once the birds flew off for five days and came back together on the sixth, and Jajali did not move.
In time, for many days all the birds did not return, when they were fully grown.
Once, after a month, the birds flew up and did not come back, king; then Jajali set out.
When they were gone, Jajali, filled with wonder, thought, "I am perfected," and pride entered him.
Seeing the birds gone out, the restrained one, honoured in himself, honouring himself, became very pleased then.
Bathing in the river, offering to the fire, the great ascetic approached the rising sun.
Honouring the sparrows on his head, Jajali, best of mutterers, clapped in the sky, saying, "I have attained dharma."
Then a voice came from the sky, and Jajali heard it: "You are not equal in dharma, Jajali, to Tuladhara.
The greatly wise Tuladhara is established in Varanasi; even he does not deserve to speak as you do, twice-born."
Fallen under the sway of impatience, the sage wandered the earth, king, where he dwelt at dusk, wishing to see Tuladhara.
After a great time he came to the city of Varanasi and saw Tuladhara selling wares.
He, seeing the brahmana coming, the dealer in goods rose up, very glad, and honoured him with welcome.
[Tuladhara said:] "You have come, brahmana; I knew it, without doubt. Hear the word I tell you, best of the twice-born.
You performed great austerity at the seashore, and you did not know the name of dharma before.
Then, through the perfection of your austerity, birds were soon born on your head, brahmana, and honoured by you.
When they were fledged and went out here and there to feed, thinking dharma came from sparrows, you heard a voice in the sky about me, best of the twice-born.
Fallen under the sway of impatience, you have come here; what shall I do that you like? Tell me, best of the twice-born."
Selling all juices and all scents, plants, herbs and their roots and fruits,
you have gained a final understanding; whence has this come to you? Tell me all that fully, greatly wise one.
Thus addressed by the famous brahmana, the trader Tuladhara, knower of the truth of dharma and wealth, satisfied with knowledge, spoke subtle things of dharma to the ascetic Jajali.

I know, Jajali, dharma with its secret, eternal, for the good of all beings, friendly, ancient, which people know.
